A variety is going to work best so she can experiment and find things she likes. You want to be careful not to paint a one-dimensional picture of gaming so you don't want to corner her into one genre. Giving her a few basic games like Mario or Rayman or other platformers that tend to have very basic controls and a clear task is a good idea. That said, don't be afraid to throw in a few "complex" games so long as they aren't dauntingly hard (so something like Borderlands or Bioshock would be fine, but maybe avoid throwing her into Dark Souls). Also, if you have any co-op games you guys can play together, she might get more fun out of that. Just try to give her as many options as possible and let her discover her own path and offer a hand when she needs it because she's almost certainly going to have questions.

Personal recommendation? Crash Bandicoot.

You want to go with something bright and fun and easy to get into. If you have a PS4 you need to get Rayman Legends, she'll love the cutsey cartoony style and the music (most likely). I bought a WiiU for exactly this type of thing. My girlfriend is like a lot of girls out there. She had only played video games a handful of times and she sucked at it and so she was discouraged about it and never tried again. The key to getting girls into video games is a welcoming and fun atmosphere. You have to make the experience similar to how you experienced your first games. All the way back to when you were younger on your first console playing your first games. For me that was super mario world on the Snes but I also remember playing a lot of Mario Kart 64 with my friends and siblings so I had heard a lot of the new Mario Kart on the WiiU and went and bought the bundle pack. I knew I would like the games at least and I hoped my girlfriend would give it a shot and she did. I live with my girlfriend and our female roommate and both of them love playing a grand pri or two on Mario kart. They never want to play for long but it's nice to flip on the WiiU and put in a few races with them. Now they of course sucked at the beginning but I never brought it up and I'd go easy on them to increase their confidence and overall just making sure that it was always fun or constructional. We continued playing on the easiest difficulty until they started grasping drifting and then the rest was easy. Now we play on the harder difficulties and speed. So in my opinion and experience you need to start them off on a game that is both fun and easy as well as something you can play together. The WiiU had plenty of couch co-op games so I got it. Now my girlfriend plays not only Mario kart with me but smash brothers, super Mario 3d world and I'm always looking for more couch co-op games to play so I can play them with her.

In a general guideline sense, I think it really depends on what sort of entertainment she likes in other mediums. Does she like doing crosswords and sudoku, assembling a huge jigsaw puzzle, reading/watching long form narrative content (Lost, Breaking Bad, GoT, etc.) or bite-sized episodic material?

Think about what it is that she likes in those things and try to look for games that might scratch the same itch.

Also, it might be worth considering a game that you yourself aren't very familiar with, so that theres less temptation to overwhelm her by going into "talkative tour-guide mode" as you explain all the details you already know by heart. I say that because I am incredibly susceptible to this myself, and I have to remind myself that part of why I like many of my favorite games was that sense of exploring something for myself, and it's really easy to accidentally take that away from someone.

As a more concrete suggestion, point & click adventure games were always the group game of choice for my family growing up. The games aren't dependent on the controls, so "spectators" don't feel like their missing out, and it's easy for everyone to crowd around and participate. Riven, Nancy Drew, The Crystal Key, and an old educational game called Bioscopia are at the center of a lot of good family memories. They worked really well for us because they have a comfortable pace, interesting stories, loads of cool art and places to explore, puzzles to solve and things for people to remember (we even had a rotating Scribe position for the harder games, and I've still got some of the notepads full of cryptic sketches from the Myst series).
